title: You need exactly-once across a database write and a Kafka publish — why don't Kafka transactions cover this, and what is the fix (transactional outbox)?
shortTitle: You need exactly-once across a database write and a Kafka publish — why don't Kafka transactions cover this, and what is the fix (transactional outbox)?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka transactions are atomic only across Kafka itself; they coordinate writes to Kafka topics and consumer offset commits within a single Kafka transaction, but they have no visibility into or control over an external database. When you must write a row to your database and publish an event to Kafka as one atomic unit, Kafka transactions cannot span both systems because there is no shared transaction coordinator across the database and the broker, and a reliable distributed two-phase commit across them is impractical. The standard fix is the transactional outbox pattern: in one local database transaction you write both the business row and an outbox row, and a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, so the database is the single source of truth for whether the event exists.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must do two things together when Rajesh transfers money: update his account ledger in the vault's ledger book, and send a notice to the central clearing house. The ledger book is the database and the clearing house is Kafka. Kafka's own "all or nothing" guarantee only covers the clearing house's internal paperwork; it knows nothing about the vault's ledger book. If the clerk updates the ledger and then the line to the clearing house drops before the notice is sent, the two are now out of sync. The outbox fix is: in the same trip to the ledger book, the clerk writes both the ledger entry and a note in an "outbox" column saying a notice must be sent, as one signature. A separate messenger later reads the outbox and sends the notice to the clearing house, and only crosses it off once it is confirmed sent. The ledger book is the one place that decides whether the notice is owed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka transactions are atomic only within Kafka, so for atomicity across a database write and a Kafka publish you use the transactional outbox — write the business row and an outbox row in one local DB transaction, then a relay publishes the outbox at least once with an idempotency key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka transactions are atomic only across Kafka itself; they coordinate writes to Kafka topics and consumer offset commits within a single Kafka transaction, but they have no visibility into or control over an external database. When you must write a row to your database and publish an event to Kafka as one atomic unit, Kafka transactions cannot span both systems because there is no shared transaction coordinator across the database and the broker, and a reliable distributed two-phase commit across them is impractical. The standard fix is the transactional outbox pattern: in one local database transaction you write both the business row and an outbox row, and a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, so the database is the single source of truth for whether the event exists.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India must do two things together when Rajesh transfers money: update his account ledger in the vault's ledger book, and send a notice to the central clearing house. The ledger book is the database and the clearing house is Kafka. Kafka's own "all or nothing" guarantee only covers the clearing house's internal paperwork; it knows nothing about the vault's ledger book. If the clerk updates the ledger and then the line to the clearing house drops before the notice is sent, the two are now out of sync. The outbox fix is: in the same trip to the ledger book, the clerk writes both the ledger entry and a note in an "outbox" column saying a notice must be sent, as one signature. A separate messenger later reads the outbox and sends the notice to the clearing house, and only crosses it off once it is confirmed sent. The ledger book is the one place that decides whether the notice is owed.

**One line to remember:** Kafka transactions are atomic only within Kafka, so for atomicity across a database write and a Kafka publish you use the transactional outbox — write the business row and an outbox row in one local DB transaction, then a relay publishes the outbox at least once with an idempotency key.

sections.s2_technical:
To see why Kafka transactions do not cover this, you have to be precise about their scope. A Kafka transaction, driven by a transactional producer, gives atomicity over two things: records written to one or more Kafka topics and partitions, and the offsets committed for messages the same producer consumed. That is the consume-process-produce loop, and within it Kafka gives you effectively-once semantics. The transaction coordinator and the commit markers it writes are entirely inside Kafka. A relational database has its own completely separate transaction manager. There is no shared coordinator that can atomically commit both, and trying to bolt on a classic distributed two-phase commit across a database and a broker is fragile, slow, and not supported by Kafka's model. So the moment your unit of work spans both a database and Kafka, Kafka transactions alone cannot make them atomic.

The naive approaches and why they fail are worth naming. If you write to the database first and then publish to Kafka, a crash between the two leaves a committed database row with no event ever published, which is a lost event. If you publish to Kafka first and then write to the database, a crash between the two leaves an event consumers already acted on but no database row, which is a phantom event. Wrapping both in a try-catch does not help, because the failure can happen in the gap after one side has durably committed. This is the classic dual-write problem, and there is no ordering of two independent commits that makes it safe.

The transactional outbox pattern solves it by removing the dual write. You give your database an outbox table. When you perform the business operation, you write the business change and an outbox row that represents the event you want to publish, both inside the same local database transaction. Because it is one transaction in one database, it is truly atomic: either both the business row and the outbox row commit, or neither does. Now there is exactly one durable fact about whether the event should exist, and it lives in your database. A separate process, the message relay, reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, marking each as published once Kafka acknowledges. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, it will republish on restart, so publication is at-least-once, which is why each outbox row carries a unique id used as the Kafka message key or header so downstream consumers deduplicate. The result is end-to-end exactly-once effect: the event is published if and only if the business transaction committed, and it is applied once despite at-least-once delivery.

There are two common ways to implement the relay. The polling publisher periodically queries the outbox table for unpublished rows, publishes them in order, and marks them published; it is simple and database-agnostic. The log-tailing approach, often called change data capture, uses a tool such as Debezium to tail the database's transaction log and stream outbox inserts to Kafka without polling, which is lower latency and lower load on the database. Here is the heart of the business side in Spring, showing the single local transaction:

```java
@Transactional // ONE local DB transaction — atomic for both writes
public void transfer(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount) {
    accountRepo.debit(from, amount);                 // business row
    accountRepo.credit(to, amount);                  // business row
    outboxRepo.save(new OutboxEvent(UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
            "TransferCompleted", buildPayload(from, to, amount))); // outbox row
    // No Kafka call here. If the DB commit fails, nothing is written anywhere.
}
```

Senior-level nuances: first, order and ordering keys matter, so the relay typically publishes in outbox insertion order and keys events so per-aggregate ordering is preserved. Second, because delivery is at-least-once, consumers must be idempotent using the outbox event id, which ties back to the earlier point that business-level exactly-once is the consumer's responsibility. Third, you must manage outbox growth by deleting or archiving published rows, often with a retention job, so the table does not bloat. Fourth, change data capture decouples the relay from application code entirely and survives application crashes gracefully, which is why it is the preferred relay at scale, though it adds operational components. Fifth, the inbound side has a mirror pattern called the inbox, where a consumer records processed event ids transactionally with its state change, giving the same exactly-once effect on the receiving end.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India processes transfers in a service that must both persist the ledger change and publish a TransferCompleted event so downstream systems update statements and send notifications. Rajesh (SAV2001) transfers to Priya (CUR3001).

Problem 1 — the first implementation wrote the ledger to the database and then published to Kafka. One day the broker was briefly unreachable right after the database commit, so Rajesh's balance changed but no TransferCompleted event was ever published. Priya's statement never updated and no notification went out. This is the dual-write lost-event failure, and Kafka transactions could not have prevented it because they do not cover the database.

Problem 2 — a developer proposed publishing to Kafka first and then writing the database, but we realized a crash in the gap would create a phantom event that consumers act on with no backing ledger entry. This made it clear no ordering of two independent commits is safe, so we adopted the transactional outbox.

Our runnable demo models a `Database` with a transaction boundary, an `OutboxTable`, a `TransferService` that writes the ledger and the outbox atomically, and an `OutboxRelay` that publishes to a `KafkaBroker` at least once and marks rows published, with a `DedupConsumer` that applies each event once by id. We inject a crash between the two writes in the naive version to show the lost event, then show the outbox version surviving the same crash. The classes are `OutboxDemo`, `Database`, `OutboxEvent`, `TransferService`, `OutboxRelay`, `KafkaBroker`, and `DedupConsumer`.

The SQL that makes the outbox possible:

```sql
-- V1__create_outbox_tables.sql (Flyway migration)
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id       VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    balance  DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    id           VARCHAR(40) PRIMARY KEY,          -- idempotency key for consumers
    aggregate_id VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,             -- e.g. accountId, for ordering key
    type         VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,             -- TransferCompleted
    payload      TEXT NOT NULL,
    published    BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    created_at   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, balance) VALUES
    ('SAV2001', 1000000.00),
    ('CUR3001', 250000.00);
```

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:

  kafka:

    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
outbox:

    poll-interval-ms: 500
    batch-size: 200
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of fifty thousand from Rajesh to Priya that must both update the ledger and publish a TransferCompleted event.

Step 1 (naive path): The service begins a database transaction, applies the debit and credit, and commits. The ledger is now durably changed.

Step 2 (naive path): Before the separate Kafka publish runs, the process crashes or the broker is unreachable. The event is never published. Rajesh's balance changed but Priya's statement never updates and no notification is sent. Kafka transactions cannot help here because the database commit happened entirely outside Kafka's scope.

Step 3 (outbox path): The service begins one database transaction and writes the ledger rows and an outbox row carrying a unique event id, then commits. Because it is a single local transaction, either both the ledger and the outbox row commit or neither does. There is now exactly one durable fact that the event is owed.

Step 4 (outbox path): The relay reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes to Kafka. In the demo it crashes right after publishing but before marking the row as published, so on restart it republishes the same event. Publication is therefore at-least-once, and the duplicate is expected.

Step 5 (outbox path): The consumer applies each event keyed by the outbox event id. The first copy is applied, updating the statement and sending the notification; the duplicate is recognized by its id and skipped. The net effect is exactly-once: the event exists if and only if the ledger committed, and it is applied once.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka transactions do not cover a database write plus a Kafka publish because their atomicity is scoped entirely to Kafka. A Kafka transaction makes writes to Kafka topics and the consumer offset commits atomic together, all coordinated by Kafka's own transaction coordinator and commit markers. Your relational database has a completely separate transaction manager, there is no shared coordinator across the two systems, and a real distributed two-phase commit across a database and a broker is impractical and unsupported. So the instant your unit of work spans both, Kafka transactions alone cannot make them atomic.

This matters because the naive dual write is unsafe in both orderings. If you write the database first and then publish, a crash in the gap gives you a committed row with no event, a lost event. If you publish first and then write the database, a crash in the gap gives you an event consumers already acted on with no backing row, a phantom event. On the National Bank of India transfer service we actually lost events this way: the ledger committed, the broker was briefly unreachable, and the TransferCompleted event was never published, so statements and notifications silently fell out of sync.

The fix is the transactional outbox pattern, which removes the dual write. In one local database transaction I write both the business change and an outbox row that represents the event I want to publish. Because it is a single transaction in a single database it is truly atomic, so either both the ledger and the outbox row commit or neither does, and now the database is the single source of truth for whether the event is owed. A separate relay then reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, marking each as published once acknowledged. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, it republishes on restart, so delivery is at-least-once, and that is why each outbox event carries a unique id that consumers use to deduplicate, giving an end-to-end exactly-once effect.

In production I choose between two relays. The polling publisher simply queries the outbox for unpublished rows and is dead simple and database-agnostic. At scale I prefer log-tailing with change data capture using Debezium, which tails the database transaction log and streams outbox inserts to Kafka with lower latency and no polling load, fully decoupled from application code. I preserve per-aggregate ordering by keying events on the aggregate id, I keep consumers idempotent on the event id, and I run a retention job to archive published outbox rows so the table does not bloat. The one-sentence principle I give the team is that Kafka transactions give you atomicity inside Kafka, and the outbox pattern gives you atomicity between your database and Kafka, and you need both to get real end-to-end exactly-once.
